did_you_know.text: The phrase “land of the people of the east” is a general term for the region east of Canaan, not the name of a specific country.
Wells were central to the lives of shepherds because they supplied water for both people and flocks in dry regions.
The verb “they rolled” is related to the Hebrew word for “wheel”: the stone was moved by rolling it, not simply by lifting it.
Haran was an ancient city in northern Mesopotamia, in the area of southeastern Turkey today.
The name Rachel means “ewe,” a young female sheep, fitting her description as a shepherdess.
The phrase “Leah’s eyes were soft” is ambiguous: it may describe delicate, tender, or weak eyes, so translations differ.
The phrase “like a few days” is a poetic way of saying that the seven years of work passed quickly for Jacob because of his love for Rachel.
Weddings in the ancient Near East were community events, which is why Laban gathered the local people for the feast.
The word “shavua” here means a period of seven days and is connected to the number seven, not to an oath.
In the Bible, the word “hated” can also mean “less loved,” not necessarily someone who is literally despised.
The name Reuben echoes the words “see” and “son,” so the verse connects it with God seeing Leah’s suffering.
The name Judah is connected with the verb “to give thanks,” meaning to praise and recognize goodness, which explains Leah’s words about his name.
